utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Mr. Krajisnik, before I give an opportunity to Mr. Tieger to continue the cross-examination, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps for your information, the Chamber has decided that in compensation of the fact that you didn't have the full number of days, also thinking about yesterday and some calculations we made, that you'll have two sessions tomorrow morning in addition to today's session. So therefore, Mr. Josse, then the last session, unless we are dealing with procedural matters, you'll have an opportunity to start re-examination. I take it that you'd like to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had assumed that re-examination was going to take place after questions from the Bench. Bearing in mind the amount of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We said we would split it up. We didn't say anything about the sequence. But I take it for one session tomorrow -- well, let's discuss it perhaps later today. We -- I think we never announced that we would do it in a different sequence apart from how much time to spend on it. But I take it that you certainly would have questions in re-examination for the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There will be some re-examination. It is a subject I would like to return to sometime today, if the Court would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we then also like to hear from you how much time you had in mind that you would need for re-examination. Not saying that whatever you say that the Chamber will grant it but at least that we know what your wishes are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, could I think about the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will need to address the Court on this subject again tomorrow -- I beg your pardon, later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Later today. Okay. Then we will hear from you later today. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Krajisnik, we were focusing on the issue of prisoners of war and detainees, camps and exchanges. We ended the session, as I recall, looking briefly at the 17th Session of the RS Assembly in the latter part of July 1992 and, in particular, the comments of Dr. Karadzic about the territories controlled and by Mr. Milanovic about the huge problem with captured people of other nationalities, Croats and Muslims. We had also focused, as I indicated, on the pace at which exchanges were occurring, and assertions that the rate of exchanges or pace of exchanges was slow, even before that time. I'd like, then, to turn our attention to tab 288 in connection with another comment about the pace of exchanges in mid-part of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is P1033.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1033 is a confidential report from Colonel Vukelic of the 1st Krajina Corps to the 1st Krajina Corps command, and if we turn our attention to -- excuse me, I should restate that. It is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps command regarding the current political and security situation in the 1st Krajina Corps zone of responsibility and sent to the command. And if we look at page 2 of the English, the last paragraph, and page 3 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik, the top of the -- the second-to-last paragraph, Colonel Vukelic indicates the current situation regarding prisoners and exchanges. "The exchange of prisoners of war with HV representatives has been quite successful but exchanges of Muslim prisoners are proceeding slowly because no one is interested in them. There are more than 2500 prisoners in the POW camp of the 1st Krajina Corps but the number --"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be the wrong page because that passage is not on the page you've indicated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's on page 3 actually. That's the next page, sorry. Yes. It's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Mr. Tieger said. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I got the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll direct your attention again. The report states that: "The exchange of prisoners of war with HV representatives has been quite successful but exchanges of Muslim prisoners are proceeding slowly because no one is interested in them. There are more than 2500 prisoners in the POW camp of the 1st Krajina Corps, but the number of detainees in Omarska, Prijedor and Trnopolje is much higher. The local authorities are slow in determining what crimes they are responsible for and want to shift responsibility to the military organs." Now, as we -- as I asked you yesterday and as you indicated, there were a number of concerns expressed about the pace of exchanges. This, Mr. Krajisnik, is another complaint or acknowledgement of the fact that Muslims and -- Muslim and Croat detainees remained in camps awaiting exchange because the exchange process was not proceeding as fast as it might otherwise, for various reasons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's right. It seems so from this paper, but I know that on the 7th of July an agreement was signed with the Muslim side on exchange of prisoners that was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was an all-for-all agreement, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have produced it to you and the Trial Chamber today. That agreement was signed under the aegis of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that agreement or any other agreements regarding exchange were intended to have Muslim and Croat prisoners held by Serbs sent to the Muslim side and vice versa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an exchange means that each side gets their fellow countrymen back. Yes. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to look next at some of the other officials of Republika Srpska who knew about prisoners, knew that Muslims and Croats were being arrested and rounded up and knew that there was, as Mr. Milanovic said, a huge problem with prisoners. If we could look next at tab 291?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P763C tab 39, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe this was the subject of discussion in earlier parts of the case, Mr. Krajisnik, so the Court and you may be familiar with it, but it is a summary of a meeting of MUP officials on July 11th, 1992, a strictly confidential report or analysis by the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of Internal Affairs. And if we look at the first page of that document, we can see some of the people in attendance. I won't go over all of them but I will indicate a few names including: Mico Stanisic, the Minister of Internal Affairs; Cedo Kljajic, the Under-Secretary of Public Security; Mr. Skipina, the Under-Secretary of the State Security Service; various assistant ministers, including Mr. Kusmuk, Mr. Planojevic, Radomir Njegus, Predrag Jeguric; and various other regional officials, including Mr. Zupljanin, Mr. Vukovic, Mr. Bjelosevic, Mr. Cvijetic, Dragan Kijac, Krsto Savic and so on. And if we could at the beginning of the -- of his introductory remarks on page 4 of the English, and I believe page 1852 of your version, Mr. Stanisic indicates that among other things, the members of the MUP have been involved and given their lives, as he says, to "liberate the occupied territories." But what I wanted to direct your attention to, Mr. Krajisnik, was page 8 of the English, at the very top of that page, and in the B/C/S, page 1855, the second paragraph or the first full paragraph of that page. At that point of the meeting, Mr. Zupljanin is addressing the group, and he notes the following: "The army and Crisis Staffs, wartime Presidencies, demand gathering as many Muslims as possible and leave such non-defined camps to the internal affairs. The conditions in these camps are poor. There is no food. Some individuals do not comply with the international standards because, among other things, the concentration centres are not appropriate or for other reasons." Mr. Bjelosevic speaks next. That's at -- he begins at page 9 of the English, and at page 1856 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, and he begins by noting, after the first two comments he makes, that, as Mr. Stanisic alluded to earlier, the police had a great share in liberating the Serb territory. And then he goes on shortly after, himself, to point out the same issue that Mr. Zupljanin had raised. That's found, Your Honours, at page 10 of the English, in the third hyphenated passage, the third from the top. And Mr. Krajisnik, on page 1857, the fifth paragraph down, where he says: "The people that the army arrests or captures are brought over in groups and left without any documents regarding reasons for the arrest." And finally, if we can turn to the last page of the document, at page 27 of the English and page 1877 of your version, we find another of the conclusions reached at the meeting regarding issues or problems identified by that gathering of senior MUP officials. And among them are the one seen immediately before the end of the document, that is before the -- it's the penultimate comment on page 27 of the English: "Solving the question of the moving out of certain inhabitants, villages, et cetera, which is not the jurisdiction of the MUP but some are trying to attribute it to the MUP." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, those are all reflections of the same circumstances and events that both Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Milanovic were referring to at the 17th Session. That is, the "liberation" of extensive portions of territory by the Bosnian Serb military forces and the resulting -- the rounding up of Muslims and Croats and their placement into various camps and the logistical and other problems resulting from that. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm seeing this for the first time today, all this that you've shown me. I wasn't aware of it then. I can only speculate whether that's right or not. I can only tell you that more Serbs left Muslim territories than Muslims left Serb territories. And of course there were prisoners from both sides. Today I've produced an order written by Mr. Stanisic related precisely to this, that prisoners should be treated according to regulations, that they should be separated from troops, et cetera. At that time, I didn't know about any of this. Either that or this meeting. However, I located a document, and I've produced it for you and for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have suggested earlier in your testimony that Mico Stanisic was unaware of the existence of camps in which large numbers of Muslims and Croats were held. Can I take it that your review of this document now satisfies you that Mr. Stanisic was very much aware of the existence of camps in which Muslims and Croats were held at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said yesterday. There is a document of the 24th of August and another one of the 28th of August where he addresses centres with a request to inform him whether camps exist, where the camps are, who is in them and in what conditions. That's the basis for what I'm saying. At the time, I had no knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just to draw your attention to the fact that you're now referring to documents that were produced, as you said, and I see one of them is among the documents you gave to the parties this morning, late August, whereas Mr. Tieger's questions are about -- are about early and mid-July, and this Chamber has heard some evidence on what happened early August, which changed -- at least seems to have changed the attention paid to camps. So therefore, referring to a late August document might not be an answer to what Mr. Tieger is putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm saying that I don't know anything about this, that I didn't know anything about it at the time, and I've said that I have submitted documents, the agreement, everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we saw yesterday, on June 10th, the Presidency sought information on detainees and a proposal of measures which you indicated it did not receive until months later, at least until the late August reports to which you're referring. Did you or any other member of the Presidency, as far as you know, speak to Mr. Stanisic in between -- during that period, to find out what was happening with detainees?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody had their own province of work. I did not talk about this. I could learn what was mentioned at the consultative meetings, and I concluded, on the basis of the documents, that the Presidency had not been informed until the 11th of August. Before the 11th of August there was no report, as far as I managed to see in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, as the Court alluded to earlier, the Presidency was informed before the 11th of August because the entire world was informed before the 11th of August, when ITN and the Guardian reporter entered the Omarska camp and sent dispatches and videos which were distributed worldwide. You know about that event.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. Mr. Ostojic took the journalists there, and we have an excerpt from the Kozarski Vjesnik. He said there was no censorship. His impression was different from the impression gained by the journalists. Also there was this press release of the government stating that what the journalists wrote about is not true. You still have this press release there. You have it here today. That's what I found out. The journalists wrote about it and then a team was sent out to check whether this was true. Commissions were sent out to see whether this was correct. Journalists went together with Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Bozanic to tour all the camps, all of them. I can bring Mr. Ostojic's statement from that time. I found it in Kozarski Vjesnik. The journalists didn't go out on their own. They went with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look next at tab 287, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, tab 287 is P583, tab 77, P447.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is a document from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior entitled report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead dated 17 July 1992. And it was directed to the president of the Presidency and the Prime Minister. So Mr. Krajisnik, this is a report which followed less than a week after the meeting of top MUP officials during which the discussion about the roundup of Muslims and Croats and their placement into camps in poor conditions took place. And it begins, in fact, by referring to that particular meeting, on the first page, the Minister of the Interior called the meeting held in Belgrade on 11 July 1992, as part of an ongoing analysis of the situation. And on page 3 of the English, and page 3 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, or the ERN ending in 6858, at the very top of the page, in English, and the very top of the page in B/C/S, Mr. Stanisic reports to the president of the Presidency and the president of the government: "The army Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible and they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor. There is no food. Individuals sometimes do not observe international norms." He also notes further down the page: "For the benefit of the president of the Presidency and the president of the government," about three paragraphs down, at the very beginning: "It should also be noted that new territories are being liberated in combat." And finally he raises to the recipients, to his superiors, the issue that was also raised and that I pointed out to you in the July 11th meeting found at page -- at the bottom of page 6 and in English and the last sentence of the first paragraph on page 11 in B/C/S. And in English, Your Honours, at page 6, that would be the last sentence before the next -- before the two-sentence paragraph at the bottom begins, so it's the last sentence of the last full paragraph. "Special emphasis should be placed" -- I'll quote that actually. "Special emphasis should be placed on the issue of relocating certain citizens, villages, et cetera, because this does not fall within the competence of the MUP, although efforts are being made to link it to the MUP." Mr. Krajisnik, contrary to the assertions you were making before, not only did Mr. Stanisic know about camps in July of 1992, but he duly reported to his superiors, to the Presidency and to the government, about the existence of camps, about the condition of those camps, about the logistical problems resulting from having so many prisoners, and about the concern about the MUP being responsible for relocating villages.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't know about this report. But it would be a good thing to see whether the government or the Presidency did something on account of this. I believe they did. Because you simply cannot turn a deaf ear to a report like this. You should just have a look at the sessions that followed after this. He's conveying what he heard at a meeting from particular individuals. Another thing: It seems to me that there was an additional page in this report, as far as I can remember, when I first looked at it, a note made by Karadzic -- well, maybe I've made a mistake, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when was that, Mr. Krajisnik, that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I think it's that information Mr. Adnan and there was a note there. I confused the two reports. There was one report with a note at the end on the situation in Semberija. It would be a good thing to see whether something had been done about this. If I had the sessions here, I would know whether the government or the Presidency did something about it. I can look this up in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it still your testimony, Mr. Krajisnik, that by the time of this report, you knew nothing about the existence of camps in which large numbers of Muslims and Croats who had been rounded up were detained in poor conditions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I will be very specific as to what I've said. I knew about -- I knew about prisoners and prisons but I did not know what conditions they lived in or who detained them. I will remind you that this Assembly session that was held on the 11th of August, and that's when a MP asked to have a debate on this. I asked the government to submit a report, some information, rather, and that the next day, on the 12th, in Banja Luka we discussed this. They did not have a report. We could not discuss it on the 12th of August, 1992 because there was no government report. That is my knowledge. That is what I heard at the assemblies. All of that did not include a government report, so I could not have any officially based knowledge from an official agency. I did not know under what conditions they lived, what camps there were and so on and so forth. Actually, nobody knew about this. You also have the statement of Mrs. Plavsic that she didn't know about it at the time either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Tieger has put to you two documents, the one in which the -- it is reported about conditions in camps, and then another report which in exactly the same terms literally the same, from -- at least from what I understand from the translation, describes again, and it is addressed to the Presidency, that there was no food, that conditions were poor. So if you say no one knew about it, sounds surprising, in view of these two reports, even if they were not addressed to the Assembly. You're saying no one knew about it, whereas in these reports, people who are drafting these reports clearly seemed to show that they were aware. So I'm trying to understand your testimony that no one knew about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I knew, no one knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And today, you still think that no one knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether anybody knew. Well, probably someone did know but I don't know. Let me just tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, let me just -- you say "someone." Now, we have a document here which is dated 17th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: July, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 17th of July. If you say "someone," I mean not every individual citizen just wrote a report to the Presidency, would they? And we know that since exactly the same language is used, that those who have read those earlier lines most likely are the ones who drafted or perhaps I should even say copied those lines into this report of the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this same minister on the 24th of August asked for information about the camps. I've submitted that to you. It also happened on the 28th of August. He asked for a reports on the camps. I did not see this. I didn't see that either. But I submitted it. Now, I can say that this is correct, but at that time, I did not know, because commissions would not be sent out had there been information about this. Commissions were sent out to tour the entire area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's known. I was just focusing on that you said no one knew it, whereas --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right. I'm sorry. Let me explain. There was a statement here made by Mrs. Plavsic. She said no one knew, including Mr. Dodik, when he testified. So I said on the basis of that, well, obviously somebody knew that this existed. Those are the words I used. Because somebody should have informed me. There were suspicions, and that's why the commission was sent out to have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Krajisnik, there were suspicions. I mean, it's described in this report, the 17th of July report, addressed to the president of the Presidency, and I mean, these reports did not come from lower-ranking persons. They came from these sub-top level and were addressed to the president of the Presidency and the Prime Minister, and to say that there were some suspicions, it doesn't say -- these reports do not say there are suspicions that there was insufficient food. It just said that there is not -- it doesn't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, some concerns with respect about this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I ask rhetorically, and with respect, why it matters what Mr. Krajisnik is now saying about whether people had suspicion at the time. His state of knowledge at the time is clearly vital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But what he's now asserting, as to whether people knew at the time and his view based on these documents as to the state of knowledge at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, Mr. Josse, I don't have to explain to you that examination of a witness can pertain to several aspects, that is to find out about the facts, to find out about reliability, credibility of a witness. And if a witness says no one knew, if we have two or three or four reports, I think it's only fair to put it to him that no one -- might be very strong language for something which was put on paper, not once but twice, in exactly the same wordings, by high ranking officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Unless the Chamber says it goes to credibility in my submission it can't assist at all, bearing in mind the Court is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not have to explain what it exactly -- and say I am now putting a question to you because I don't want to know about the facts and then the next question to say, well, this is a question which relates to -- I mean, that's in the Chamber's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I won't pursue my objection at the moment, but I do reserve the right to raise it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do. Of course, you -- that's understood and accepted. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was merely on my feet to say that that was a completely appropriate line of questioning for a variety of reasons but I don't need to go into the details now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, you're not challenging the reality of this document, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not challenging the information, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second point, then. Given the professional relationships that you might have had with the president of the Presidency and with the Prime Minister, how can you explain that these people didn't tell you about what was in this report? I would like to go a bit further, if you allow me. I mean, in this report, there are, I mean, very important, very striking elements, for the life of a country. I mean, the people who read this report must have been moved by it. So how can you explain the fact that they didn't even talk to you about it? You have to understand me here. Outside, you know, any report of hierarchy or institutional relationships, whatsoever. I mean in every day life, in routine life, there are always this kind of relationship where you can go and see -- I've just had this -- I've just received this document, it's -- what do you think about it? What can we do? How can we react to this? So how can you explain that these people didn't talk to you about this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't understand why they would tell me about this. It is their job to get this done, to take measures, to punish, to investigate. All of that is up to them, the government. If the Prime Minister got this, then he was the only one who was supposed to take care of this, and the MUP and the military. If I were informed about everything, I'd have to be like a computer. I assure you, in the papers there is everything about this, when we discussed it and when we said explicitly that everything that was going on in these camps, these prisons, had to be investigated. You have the transcripts where I was present. This wasn't written today. It was written 12 or 14 years ago. And then tasks were given to take measures urgently, to punish perpetrators and so on and so forth. I haven't got the transcripts here in front of me, but I know that the Presidency took a very firm stand to investigate the facts and to establish the facts. I was present there. For me, it was sufficient that they would take care of it. They received all this information from the field. The commission was there, everything was supposed to be established by that commission, and to provide official information. Not to have hearsay but to have proper information. Nobody else was authorised but the government, the military, the president of the republic. It wasn't my job. I'm not disassociating myself from it, but I did hundreds of things about which I did not inform the Prime Minister, who was 20 kilometres away from me. If somebody discussed something, well, measures were taken. I can guarantee that measures were taken in respect of this but we just have to find this. There is a request from Mr. Stanisic precisely from that period, where he rigorously orders the centres how they should behave. I handed in that document today. I found it by chance. That's probably it. Somebody gave him instructions, do this or do that. For that, that was -- for me that was sufficient. I really did not have any knowledge about the conditions in the camps. But how could I have known? How could I have known? How could I say, well, people are being killed, they have no food, they have no water, let it be. Who could I possibly have done that? I would have done my best to improve their conditions. The commission proposed all of that and this was officially done. It was submitted to the government and the Assembly was informed. Your Honour, on the 11th of August, there was no government report, and on the 12th, we could not discuss an official report by the government. I know that. I can guarantee that something was done about this. How could something not be done about this? Well, I did not take any measures. It was not for me to take any measures, and I was not kept abreast of these things either. Of course anybody would be interested in what was going on. If you wouldn't be interested in this kind of thing, then you would be committing a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find the document tomorrow in relation to this and I'll bring it to you, so that you will see what the reaction was. For sure there was a reaction. How could one not react to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we've had an opportunity just during the course of the last couple of sessions to see a number of people who knew about the camps, including every top MUP official, Colonel Ilic, Major Andric, the Prijedor Crisis Staff, the Sanski Most Crisis Staff, the Petrovac Crisis Staff, Milanovic and the entire Assembly. Now Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Mandic also knew about the existence of camps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic testified here, and he said that he did not know about them. He only knew about Kula, and he sent a commission to find out what was going on. That's what I heard him say here. As to whether he knew, he should have been asked. He testified here in this Court stating that he did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm just, for your information, while answering questions, you should keep in mind that if a witness said something, that it's not for the full 100 per cent sure that the Chamber will adopt such a testimony as in accordance with the truth if there is other evidence which contradicts that evidence. I'm just pointing that to you. Because you're using several times language that -- well, with some conviction in your voice, this is what the witness said, but of course you should be aware that in formulating your answers and telling us -- and giving your testimony, you cannot just rely on adoption by this Chamber of every single word a witness said in this Court. And in a similar way, you said, and it's not for the first time, you said, "How could I know?" Of course, that exactly is the issue. I mean, the answer to that question is very simple. You could know if those who, on paper, seemed to have been aware of certain circumstances would have told you. Of course, your evidence, we well understood that, that they did not do so. But adding to it, "How could I know," that's exactly the issue, whether they told you, whether they didn't tell you. I thought it wise to inform you about these matters, which might enable you to understand exactly what it means to receive evidence, and also that we of course, first of all, are interested in whether you knew, whether you were informed, and then the question whether you could have been informed, that it's a more complicated question and is not simply answered by saying, "How could I have possibly known?" Because that answer is -- that answer is -- or that question is simply to be answered, how you could, but most important is what happened. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at tab 286, please, which is P461. I want to turn to page 11 of the English, and it should be approximately the same page in your version, Mr. Krajisnik. It's the first reference -- well, first of all, I should indicate that this is a conversation between Mr. Mandic and Brana Kvesic on the 10th of July, 1992, also between -- also Mr. Ivo Rezo comes on the phone during the course of that conversation. And, Mr. Krajisnik, if -- I'm afraid I can't direct you immediately to the B/C/S page, but if you look at the reference at approximately the eleventh page in to Mr. Madzarevic, which is on page 2474, in approximately the middle. And, Your Honours, that's also on page 11 of the English. And then looking -- you found that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a couple of comments down, at the very -- the last two comments in -- on page 11, Mr. Kvesic says: "There are some of our men in Manjaca, man." And Mr. Mandic says: "In Krajina, right?" And they continue. "Yes," says Mr. Kvesic. Mandic says: "We can do it." Kvesic: What can you do about it? Mandic: A lot. Kvesic: Listen, fuck, let's find out ... Listen, it is because of relations in general. Mandic: Naturally, man. Kvesic: There is ... Mandic: All right, I'll tell it to my main boss." And then further on, about five or six of the lines down, Kvesic says: "They are placed somewhere on Manjaca." Mandic: Over there in the military camp on Manjaca? So, Mr. Krajisnik, it is clear that Mr. Mandic, like Mr. Stanisic, knew about the existence of camps in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he knew. If he said here that he knew, then he knew. Here he said that he didn't. Maybe he was aware of Manjaca after all. This is a reference to our first meeting in London in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Mandic both, as Dr. Djeric told the entire Assembly at the 22nd Session in November 1992, reported to Dr. Karadzic and you. Those are the two people at the top levels of government that they dealt with. And let me turn your attention to the 22nd Session at page 12. Mr. Krajisnik, for your benefit that is at page 9644, the last ERN digits in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will find that portion beginning in the second half of the first long paragraph, and I'll begin at the part "if somebody else insisted."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me address Mr. Krajisnik's attention to the passage. In the first long paragraph on page 9644, Mr. Krajisnik, at approximately the middle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I have not found it. We are talking about the 22nd Session which is the 23rd, 24th of November, 1992, and you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, it would be -- I don't know which binders the Court has. And at the beginning of the session, we -- at the beginning of Mr. Krajisnik's examination-in-chief, in fact, we distributed common binders, we had hoped, so that everybody could -- I don't know if the Court has the benefit of that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have these grey binders. To be quite honest, I don't know exactly who prepared them. But whatever has happened -- are we talking about the same session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So I do know that -- and in connection, as I indicated, and we had a discussion about this earlier in court, there was a revised translation of the 22nd Session. That came up with Mr. Stewart; I don't know if Mr. Josse was here at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have got all the material that Mr. Tieger is alluding to and we bring them into court every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, the binder I'm working on is prepared by our staff, and -- so -- but whatever confusion there is, if there is a possibility to have it. But you have the -- you say it's on the -- you gave the number because then I could look on my screen to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The ERN number, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mainly if there is any exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Exhibit number would be P65, Treanor 14, tab 213. But I don't know whether or not the revised translation has -- was entered by the Court personnel. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But here is the version -- we can put it on the ELMO, Your Honour, or the Court can look at it and decide how to handle this. And there is a yellow tab marking the particular passage we will be referring to now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's -- I know you've been looking at that while we've been talking. It's the portion that begins in the middle of that paragraph at page 12 of your version. And it -- and there, Dr. Djeric states: "If somebody else insists on appointments of certain ministers, then, gentlemen, that person needs to assume responsibility for the work of those ministers as well, so far not a single membership of state leadership did that, on the contrary, everybody says the government is responsible, the Prime Minister is responsible, orchestration is responsible, and when it comes to legislature, when we are dealing with the Minister of Justice, the Minister of the Interior, they are not even members of the government. They don't attend the government meetings. They meet with the president of the republic and the chairman of the Assembly, not a single one of them ever appeared before the people or on TV and said they were responsible for their work and what they were doing, thereby releasing the Prime Minister of any liability. That would be fair." It was certainly Mr. Djeric's understanding in November of 1992 that Stanisic and Mandic would meet with you and Dr. Karadzic rather than him or other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. And at those meetings, Mr. Krajisnik -- well, first of all, that's correct, isn't it? And I'll remind you, since you seem fond of referring to Mr. Mandic's testimony, that's what he said. It's true that Mandic and Stanisic used to go directly to you and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic didn't say that, nor did he come to see me. Neither Mr. Stanisic nor Mr. Mandic. But it's true that Mr. Djeric said this. But we also have Stanisic's and Mandic's contributions at this session. Mr. Mandic did not say that they were reporting to me or had been keeping me informed, and you can't find that bit. Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Mandic did not keep me informed. Nor did they go to my office, as Mr. Djeric says. They did not simply attend cabinet meetings, and that's why Mr. Djeric thought that they must be elsewhere, such as in the president's office or my office. After this remark, they did start coming to cabinet meetings, and you can hear other contributions by the two of them, just behind this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you've referred on quite a number of occasions to the all-for-all agreements that would enable the exchanges to move forward and appeared to be pointing the finger at the Muslims for failing to implement such agreements, that would have resulted in the -- in the prisoners and detainees in Serb detention facilities going to the Muslim side and vice versa. Now, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, one of the reasons that the exchanges were not moving forward at a different pace was that both the Muslims and the international community recognised that this was a technique or device for expulsions and tried not to cooperate. In fact, you were -- Mr. Stewart cited for you Ambassador Okun's testimony which was similar to that of other international representatives from whom this Court heard, that this represented a "terrible moral dilemma." So the fault wasn't with some kind of arbitrary lack of cooperation by the Muslim side; at least part of the problem was that people saw through this technique.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's not true. I said that I had heard from those who were doing that that Muslims were not willing to go forward with an all-for-all exchange, and I concluded that was true because the Muslims had signed one agreement but they didn't want to sign another agreement. And I submitted those. The 7th July agreement was signed and the 11th July was not signed. The mediators, in signing -- in the signing of these agreements was the UNPROFOR. That's why it was very difficult for me to say any more about these exchanges. The UNPROFOR mediated in the first agreement, for an all-for-all exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Krajisnik, that the representatives of the international community -- I'll start again. You agree, Mr. Krajisnik, that the representatives of the international community recognised that the detention of Muslims and their subsequent exchange represented a form of or a technique for ethnic cleansing and resisted participation in it for that reason?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know any examples except the one from Bosanski Brod, when Mr. Kljujic -- sorry, Kirudja was involved. I provided you with newspaper articles. And I'm not aware that the international community condemned this. I gave you also video footage about how the ethnic cleansing was done, but I was not aware that the international community thought of this as a form of ethnic cleansing or a technique, and Mr. Okun is not right about this. I was not aware that the international community was seeing it that way. And he did not tell me anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I know you were aware of the Mazowiecki report because I know that in November or December - I can't recall precisely when - you condemned it and condemned him as biased. So you knew about that report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I read it recently again. And I established that he didn't actually go to Bihac because the Muslims were shooting. He went instead to Viktor Bubanj and he had only praise for that place, whereas hundreds of people were killed. I based my statement that he was biased on other examples, and I saw from the examples I know that he was less than well informed. In Viktor Bubanj, for which he had only praise, is -- that was a place where hundreds of people were killed by criminals and he didn't even put that in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. You can tell us that you think Mr. Mazowiecki was biased or that you rejected his conclusions for whatever reason you want, but my question was whether you were aware of it. And so let's turn to Mr. Mazowiecki's report from August of 1992 which is found at tab 309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not about aware necessary, Your Honour, it's about a particular portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's P295, P583, tab 94.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 295? Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, tab 309. Did I miss --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll try to indicate the tab number specifically and then I will often be giving the exhibit number, Mr. Krajisnik, so you'll have to not be misled by that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are providing a lot of material, and it's difficult to find one's way through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll help you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm counting on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, if we can turn to page 5 of that report, in the English, it is paragraph 23, and you will find that, Mr. Krajisnik, at page 5 of the B/C/S, and helpfully the paragraphs are numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see you're at that page, Mr. Krajisnik. There, the report states: "The detention of civilians is clearly being used as a method of pressuring them to leave the territory. In many cases, after agreeing to leave, they are obliged to sign documents renouncing their claim to their homes and other property or indicating that they agree to donate their property to the local government. Ethnic Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina have also adopted the policy of 'exchanging prisoners.' According to some impartial observers the need to obtain ethnic Serbs to exchange against detained Muslims is one of the main reasons for arbitrary detention of ethnic Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina." That's a reflection, Mr. Krajisnik, of the understanding of the international community about the technique of detention and exchange and their consequent reluctance to participate in it, the "terrible moral dilemma" that Ambassador Okun referred to.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I did not read this report. I told you. I read it only in excerpts just a few days ago and I read passages about Bihac and Viktor Bubanj. At the time, however, I gave my assessment based on other things. If I had the opportunity to read the entire report, then I could perhaps comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to that particular section of the report as a reflection of what Ambassador Okun told us, other internationals told us, and we see here was the understanding of the international community. But you -- I had also asked you whether it wasn't the case that the Muslims themselves were reluctant to participate in this process for precisely the same reason, that they recognised what it was about. Now, you stated, at least once and I believe more than once, or you referred more than once during the course of your examination-in-chief, to agreements to exchange populations, and on May 24th, you referred to, at I think page 19, you said, at the local level they even discussed an exchange of the civilian population. We didn't know that at the time. They said let all our people go. We will let all your people go. And that way, people will be safe. This is in the minutes of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when Mr. Sefer Halilovic informed them of this, and you directed the Court's attention to the minutes of that Presidency session, and to Mr. Halilovic's book. It may be useful, Mr. Krajisnik, to look at that particular session in its -- a little bit more detail, to understand more fully the understanding of the Muslim side about this process and the references that you made to such local agreements. And in that connection, if we could distribute, if it isn't already available, the tape recording of the session of the Bosnian Presidency held on 20 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I'm at the court's -- I'm not suggesting that we need to break but obviously, even if we move quickly, I'll be a few minutes beyond the 10.30 time, so I didn't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I'm just looking at one -- one second, please. One question, Mr. Krajisnik. If you say that the report of Mr. Mazowiecki was biased, isn't it true that he in his report states clearly that serious violations of human rights were committed by all parties, although he says that especially the fate of the Muslims was tragic but he doesn't exclude in any way crimes committed, even says that it's what happens, by all parties. So if you're so strong in saying that he was -- it says: "Human rights violations are being perpetrated by all parties to the conflict. There are also victims on all sides." And then he continues saying that the situation of the Muslim population is particularly tragic. But if you say people were killed in Viktor Bubanj -- I mean, I'm trying to understand where, although there is some emphasis, that Mr. Mazowiecki, and we are now talking, I think, about the final report, Mr. Tieger, and we are not talking about the interim reports that were published earlier. Could you explain what made you comment so negatively on this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the only thing he said, in general terms that all three sides were to blame. And individually he only spoke about visits to the Serb territory, as if he never went to the Muslim territory. You will see that he didn't go to Bihac, he went to Viktor Bubanj. He actually commended them. I even have a report stating that he commended them. A special document. He probably wasn't even informed. I'm not trying to say that he was doing this on purpose. What you read out is just striking a balance, but on an individual basis, he only talked about the Serbs. Visits to the Serb territories. As much as I managed to see the report in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That special document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zenica, Tuzla, Mostar, Travnik. None of that is mentioned. Nothing. Only Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether that's true or not, I'll have to reread it again. But you said he actually commended them and I even have a report stating that he commended them, a special document. Are you referring to any of the interim reports or -- I'm just trying to find out so that I can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I have a special document, a separate document. The warden of the Viktor Bubanj prison stated that Mr. Mazowiecki had commended him, but it wasn't in this report. He gave a positive assessment of Viktor Bubanj. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's at least what the warden of that prison says. I mean, I thought, as a matter of fact, you were referring --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- were referring to a source which was Mr. Mazowiecki himself, but whether or not the governor or the warden of Viktor Bubanj there expressed what -- if we do not find it in the reports of Mr. Mazowiecki, of course, the question would be whether it's correct or not what this or not what this warden said or reported. But I do understand that it's not a document for which authorship is with Mr. Mazowiecki. We'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I take it that you will tell us when you're ready to address the procedural matters you had in mind, perhaps after the next break, but I just don't want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I most certainly have not forgotten the issue, Your Honour. It's foremost in my mind, but after the next break would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll do it after the next break. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just before the break, I had been directing your attention to the understanding of the international community and of the Muslim side about the technique of and consequence of exchanges, and we had been just about to look at a document which is a more complete version of something which you alluded to in your examination-in-chief, and that's the session of the BH Presidency held on 20 June 1992. Looking at page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had forgotten where we were. I think this needs a number. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1246, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Tieger, if you could tell us what day it was subject of the examination-in-chief, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in the -- this portion of the first page, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Halilovic is speaking, and beginning at about the middle of the page, he relates that his understanding of --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said on the first page but it's not on the first page. Izetbegovic, Pelivan, Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Quite right. It's page 8080 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He does direct his attention to SDS members who he refers to as extremist members of the SDS, driven around in an UNPROFOR vehicle in the Krajina, and to some kind of agreement and indications about an exchange and settlement. And he continues: "If I understand it correctly, I think that's very dangerous and fatal from a political aspect, so I would like us to take a stand about this, because we are playing directly into the hands of those whose intention it is to create some ethnic territories, to move the population and to create clean national units." And then if we look to a couple of comments by the president and -- well, by Mr. Izetbegovic on page 3 of the English, and for you, Mr. Krajisnik, beginning on page 8083 and we'll see it again on page -- the next passage on 8084. Under president, he states: "Let's return to the question, the question that Halil asked." And then continues: "There is one question, the people are in danger and the situation in Banja Luka is similar. There is the Banja Luka, Zenica, et cetera problem. They are being threatened with destruction. You can either move out and then we'll do an exchange, et cetera, and change the ethnic composition we've got. We can choose between either simply accepting this or not accepting it. If we don't accept it, then these people really can get hurt. If we accept it, we are legalising ethnic division that is..." And then continuing on the portion under the heading, Izetbegovic, on the next page for you, Mr. Krajisnik, and the last paragraph of page 3 in the English. "If we don't accept the ultimatum, these people really could be hurt. If we accept it, we are legalising ethnic division, that is the alteration of the demographic picture of Bosnia, the creation of ethnically clean territories like some precondition for the creation of some kind of a Serbian state in BH. Finally, as regards the exchange, is it fair and is it okay?" Those remarks, Mr. Krajisnik, are yet another reflection of the terrible moral dilemma to which Mr. Okun and others alluded, and the understanding of the Muslim side of the purpose and consequences of exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How the Muslim side understood this, you can see in Mr. Halilovic's conclusion, and I've submitted that. The Presidency never discussed this again. This was just for Mr. Halilovic. I would like to draw your attention to something here. Halilovic says, "Serbs from Central Bosnia are moving out. And the armed forces of the Serbs are gaining strength around Sarajevo." And that is what caused concern, as far as he was concerned. You have it all in his book. He commented on that. You have it here. I read that. I certainly did. Muslim representatives in Bihac also took part in the exchange. Perhaps you should have read that too a few moments ago. You probably saw that, what Mr. Halilovic said. The Muslims and the Serbs were agreeing on that. Regarding the relocation of the population, that is. Official organs, official authorities were agreeing on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I've been focusing on the issue of exchange to some extent, Mr. Krajisnik, so let me ask you this: It wasn't only Stanisic and Mladic and Andric and others who knew that Muslims were languishing in detention until the exchange commission completed its work and sent them to the other side. You were aware of the existence of the exchange commission and also aware of allegations that it was considered as a device through which ethnic cleansing was pursued. And that was true in May and June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just knew Mr. Mandic. I called him. I didn't even know who the members of the commission for the exchange were. When I found out from the media that ethnic cleansing was being talked about, I made a statement, a public statement, in October, that I was deeply opposed to ethnic cleansing. I said that. I was the only politician in Bosnia-Herzegovina who made such a statement. You haven't got a single statement of this kind made by any other politician except me. That's the only one I saw in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, you also said in the Club 91 interview in April of 1991, if I recall correctly, how deeply opposed you were to the division of the live tissue of Bosnia. So I think it's fair to say that at least on some occasions what you say and what you pursue or believe, may not be wholly in harmony.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. In May 1991, I was president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I deeply worked for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said everything that I thought then because what was in the making was a historical agreement between the Serbs and the Muslims. As the times changed, of course, my statements were adapted to the times, but they were never radical and they were never against a single Bosnia, because we had accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Led get back to the exchanges. The exchange commission as we saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. Mr. Krajisnik, you said: "I was the only politician at that time who publicly opposed ethnic cleansing." How should we understand that? That those who did not express themselves were not opposed against it, or should we understand this to be that -- I mean, I'm trying to find out what your testimony in this respect means, because if all the others were opposed but did not publicly express that, what's then the difference? I'm trying to understand where you put yourself in a very special position as publicly opposing against ethnic cleansing. Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said the following: When I learned from the media about the problem of ethnic cleansing, I made a public statement that I was deeply opposed to every form of ethnic cleansing. I made two statements. And I said, as far as I managed to see in the media, I am the only person who made such a statement. That is the meaning of what I've said. I don't know. Maybe I've made a mistake. Maybe somebody else made a statement to that effect, too, but I never found such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you made a mistake when you said that, but I'm asking you what it means. Because you draw our attention to the fact that you publicly state against ethnic cleansing, does that mean that the others who did not publicly state against it, that they did not care or that they did not oppose or that -- I mean, if you were the only one, I take it that the others were aware of what was published in the media as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll explain. The Prosecutor asked me about myself, whether I knew. I was explaining myself. As for others, whoever I came across and whoever I talked to from the Serb side, from the Serb leadership, I had the impression that they were opposed to that, but I don't know why they did not make public statements to that effect. Maybe they did. There were a lot of interviews but I did not read such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out whether you were asked about others and whether you introduced that yourself. You were asked about whether you were aware of the existence of the exchange commission and whether you were also aware of allegations, that is it was considered as a device through which ethnic cleansing was pursued, and you were asked whether that was true in May or June of 1992. And then no one asked you about other politicians, what they said in the media. You introduced that just by yourself. You said, "I made a statement in October," which of course does not directly relate to what was asked of you, that was about May or June of 1992. And then you introduced yourself, that you were the only one. So therefore, if you say, "I was just explaining my own position," you are comparing your own position with the position of other politicians. Did you ever discuss with others, since you gave this public statement, whether they should not do the same or if it was -- I mean, it was an important item, wasn't it? So did you ever discuss whether they should publicly express against ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mean only Serb politicians. I meant all politicians, Muslim, Croat and Serb, when I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question -- my question was about Serb politicians, just to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the media, I heard from Karadzic when he said that there was no ethnic cleansing, and this was in the month of September, after Owen and Stoltenberg, and then there are also people who were in the authorities in Banja Luka who said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's again not an answer to my question. What you -- I asked you whether you discussed with others whether they should, as you did, publicly express against ethnic cleansing. Your answer now is that in public statements they denied ethnic cleansing to take place, which, of course, is not the same, because even if it does not happen you still can say, but -- I mean, saying that it should not happen doesn't say that you admit that it does happen. At least I take it that when you publicly expressed against ethnic cleansing, that this was not admitting that it happened, or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I remember this now and I have to correct myself. In that article, Mr. Karadzic said precisely that there cannot be any ethnic cleansing in Serb territories. That's what Koljevic said too when we talked. We did talk about this problem of accusations concerning ethnic cleansing, probably. I can't remember now. So that's why I said it in some interview. And, well, I don't know whether anyone of them said something in public. Perhaps for the international media. I mean, I said that I found my own statement but I did not find any statements by others. I'm not trying to say that they didn't say anything, but we did talk about these accusations of ethnic cleansing and they were denying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you did say that you were the only one. It was translated to us that "I was the only politician in Bosnia-Herzegovina who made such a statement." So it doesn't say, "I didn't see any of the other statements." You just claimed that you were the only one. I'm trying to carefully listen to your testimony but you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You still have not answered my question. My question was whether you discussed that others should also publicly express against ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not talk about that, but I did talk about ethnic cleansing. Accusations concerning ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we looked at documentation reflecting that the exchange commission was established on the 8th of May, and it was within a short time, very short time, after that, that it was in operation. And if we can turn next to tab 259, that's a video, Your Honour, which I'd like to play. P74. And this is a video depicting the approximately 400 Muslims from Bratunac about whom we've heard before, who were expelled from Bratunac to Visoko via Pale. I'm just going to play a brief portion of that video, if we could start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we have the problem that there was no text on our screen, B/C/S was not translated, and therefore -- into English and we have no French either then. Unless the parties would agree that it is already in the -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was going to say yes, it is already in evidence. I won't be referring to the text of the video. It's been that exhibit that has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just refreshment for our visual --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct. I just wanted to identify those particular prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So long as the witness is happy, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first wait and see what the questions will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there's a transcript available, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now those prisoners and others like them, whom we just saw on the screen, were expelled from Bratunac via Pale, as we've heard on quite a number of occasions, through the process of the exchange commission, Mr. Krajisnik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who conducted the exchange of those prisoners because we only have two documents from the government here requiring certain trucks to be able to transport them to Ilijas. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I do understand that you, as being an accused, that you heard all the evidence that was presented. During your examination, what you say, I don't know who arranged for it, there is no need to make reference to other evidence that was presented here, because usually witnesses would not even know about that. You're just asked, because you're more or less commenting on the evidence which this Chamber heard, and since of course it's all very transparent, but it's not exactly within the role of a witness what you're doing at this moment to say, "I didn't know but we only have two documents." Well, whether we have two or ten or five is not something for a witness at this moment, unless you're specifically asked about what you know about the evidence presented, but it's not the subject of questioning, and you're more or less in debate at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. But I understood when he says "we've seen testimony here," but otherwise I agree. I'll try to answer the questions strictly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not dramatic, but I just wanted to point that out. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 256, Your Honours and Mr. Krajisnik. That's P61.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And although the bulk of the list consists of -- the bulk of the document consists of a long list of names, we can see, on the front page of the English and of your version as well, Mr. Krajisnik, in B/C/S, that the subject is the total of 400 persons who were driven from Bratunac to Pale, who are listed on those pages. And if we turn to page 3 of the English, and page 00835782 of the B/C/S, we can also see that the document is signed by Slobodan Markovic, member of the government's commission on behalf of the Serbian MUP for the exchange of prisoners of war. And as we noted in an earlier document, Mr. Markovic was the MUP representative on the commission for exchange at that time. So the expulsion and -- of the 400 people from Bratunac via Pale was conducted through the exchange commission, which was operating less than a week after its establishment.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see this document for the first time. I didn't read it before. It says: "Member of the government's commission on behalf of the Serbian MUP." I suppose this man was simultaneously a member of the commission and a member of the MUP. Maybe he represented both organisations. He was wearing both hats. I'm just -- I'm just saying I don't know whether the commission did this. I just don't know. It's not that I'm disputing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did you find out that the Commission for Exchange was functioning?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the commission in later years. All I knew was that Mr. Mandic did this job while he was there. I cannot remember the date when I found out that the commission was operating because there were several commissions across regions, and I didn't know about this central commission. I didn't feel its activity in 1992. Or maybe I did. I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab 279, please. That's P283, P529, tab 410.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, one moment. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 279 contains a conversation, Mr. Krajisnik, between you and your brother Mirko, on the 22nd of June, 1992. At the beginning of the conversation, we see you and Mirko talking about a copy of a document regarding the establishment of the war commission. That's on the first page. But then if we could turn to page 2 of the English and 0915 of your -- of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, that's at the beginning of the bottom half of the page for you. And, Your Honours, in English it's the same. It's the beginning of the second half of the -- of that page. Mirko Krajisnik speaking: Listen, please, apart from the thing that we talked about, what's her name, Vlatka Krsmanovic, she's some kind of professor from Sarajevo, do you know her? You say: Yes. Mirko: She is allegedly detained up there. Momcilo Krajisnik: And who wants to intervene? Mirko: Town wants her back. Mirko Pejanovic. Who? Mirko Pejanovic. He does? Yes, not him but the town. And then continuing on to the next page in both versions, Mirko says: "She is detained. Can she be exchanged so that she can come back? She is a Serb. Momcilo Krajisnik: A Serb, are you kidding? Mirko: Is she a Croat then? Momcilo: Sorry? Mirko: What is she then? I don't know. Momcilo: Okay, people here think: We have many men, so they want one woman. Let it go, Mirko, for God's sake. Pejanovic is only asking for matters that interest him. Release people from Dobrinja, that one from ... the one that Bradina has from Novi Grad. Say hello to him and tell him please that there are in Bradina ... Serbs. Let him engage a bit more as a Serb. They should let it go. Mirko: Okay, so that means ... Momcilo: ... you tell him. Mirko: Fine. Momcilo: People will be released. There is a committee for that. You should not be dealing with it. He is now on such position that ... Now, in connection with your brother's inquiry on behalf of Mr. Pejanovic about the release of someone held by the Serbs, surprisingly a Serb, you advise your brother to back off because, in part, there is a committee for that purpose. That's a reference to the Commission for Exchange, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who this woman is, and I don't know what committee is -- this is all about. All I know is that Mr. Pejanovic occasionally interceded with me to have somebody released. I did all I could and he didn't do enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please focus on the question that is put to you. You --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. -- I didn't say that you -- I asked you to focus on the question, that is to leave out what is not asked and to answer to the question asked to you. The question was whether this was the committee for exchange. Somewhere in your answer you say, "I don't know what committee it was." So the answer is simply, I can't tell you because I don't remember what the committee was I was talking about. That's the question. Not about whether you knew the woman, whether or not -- that's all --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please focus on the question and answer the questions as they are put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we just have the interpretation of what Mr. Krajisnik just said, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was speaking at the same time as the judge, so he do not get interpreted. What he said was, "That's what I said."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you said far more, and I'm trying to draw your attention to the fact that we are not have five answers, four of which are not a response to any question put to you but just to receive an answer to the question which was put to you. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it will be of assistance, then, to turn to tab 282, P292 KID, P529, tab 409. This is a conversation between you, Mr. Krajisnik, and Momcilo Mandic on the 26th of June, 1992. Perhaps to orient you, this is the day after your conversation that we looked at before, when Mr. Mandic advised you that the ociscen, the cleansing or mopping up operations, had been taken care of. In this conversation, in the early part, Milijana calls on your behalf indicating to Mr. Mandic that the president would like to speak to him. You get on the phone and say: "All right, are you a traitor as everybody else?" Mandic: God forbid. And then at the bottom of page 1 of the English, and should be about the top of page 2 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, you ask him: "Momo, tell me, how does it go?" He says: "Well, I am not up to date with what is going on in that lower part, the main one but as for this one - it is going well." And then the conversation continues about six or seven lines down. You say: "Two things. I actually wanted to see if Stanisic was there, to see with him what is happening with this, so it means that what we agreed upon was not respected." Mandic: Yes. Krajisnik: There is still a half chance today, and tomorrow it will be finished. ... Krajisnik: It's a big problem with Alija, has that one been finished, that is awful, as of today we finish it all, you know. Mandic: Here there is something pounding. Krajisnik: Huh? Mandic: It could be heard that they pound. Krajisnik: Yes, that is. Has he made it down there or not - it's all over now. Secondly, have you released the one I told you about by any chance? And before I move on to that discussion, let me just ask you a couple of quick questions, Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, the reference to Stanisic earlier in the conversation is a reference to Mico Stanisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
