utterances.text: And the pounding that Mr. Mandic referred to is artillery shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, probably, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the conversation continues, if we turn to page 3 of the English, and it would be page 0984, I believe, of your version, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, because I don't know exactly where this is going, but I'm a bit surprised my learned friend didn't read the three or four lines after where he last left off, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll be happy to do that, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It would have been incorporated, but this is just as easy a way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Secondly, have you released the one I told you about by any chance?" Mandic: "Yes, I have."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And here, Your Honours, of course we are in the middle of page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Krajisnik: Yes. Mandic: He left for Vrbanja one hour ago. Krajisnik: Thanks God. Mandic: Karamehmedovic, right? Krajisnik: Yes, that's him. Mandic: Well, he is gone. Krajisnik: Let me also ask you what about this Savic Milos, since it's his brother, that is really ... Mandic: President, I put it on the list, the first next exchange and it will be finished. Krajisnik: Check it down there, do you have anyone there, can you contact someone? As we've seen earlier, Mr. Krajisnik, that's a reference to your efforts to assist Mr. Savic in getting his family member exchanged, correct, through Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then the conversation continues on the next page, page 3 of the English, at the top. Mandic: There is this Vukovic, the member of the youth organisation, a Serb, who is criticising us because we have 400 prisoners here, you know? Krajisnik: Who is criticising? Mandic: I've got 400. Krajisnik: And who was criticising? Mandic: This Vukovic Filip, this member of youth organisation, Serb, he says, clean it, but for them they are ... Krajisnik: Filip Vukovic? Mandic: Yes. Krajisnik: Communist? Mandic: Yes, yes. Krajisnik: What does he want? Mandic: He is the president of that exchange commission. Krajisnik: Their commission? Mandic: Yes. And what is it that he wants? Mandic: War prisoners, no, they are ex for them. They are hardly interested in people, they are interested in ammunition and meat and now we let those women and children go to Vrbanja, to go to their own people, he says that's ethnic cleansing what we do. Krajisnik: He does. Mandic: ... here ... when ... I will fucking ... Krajisnik: And where is he now? Mandic: Somewhere there, I do not know. Krajisnik: With them, isn't he? Mandic: Yes. Krajisnik: That means he is theirs? Mandic: Yes, yes, yes. Krajisnik: God, traitors are all around. Mr. Krajisnik, first of all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, I don't know if this is in order, but there seems to be a considerable difference between the meaning of one of these sentences and the English translation. When Momcilo Mandic says: This Vukovic, Filip from the youth organization, Serb, says, you are clearing or cleansing, however in their eyes, they are -- that's what it says in Serbian, whereas the English translation makes it look like the youth organisation man said, "Clean it." Which seems to be quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the fifth line down from the top of page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. You'd say the imperative is now a description of what he blames that is done. Is that a correct understanding of your -- and I'm looking at the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Clean it now" is "you are cleaning or cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it helpful to read back what was just read? Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to find a way that this is now properly in our material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please -- I suggest the following to the parties, that I take the original exhibit, that I just change it with -- in the translation and add to it that "I did it" and that it's -- and I make a reference to the transcript of today where the correction was, because otherwise we have to distribute it again and again, and everyone does the same in his own copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, I would like to have the original of this exhibit. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My only question, I take it that because the interpreter was speaking, I don't know if that translation got back to Mr. Krajisnik. I presume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, the interpreters, the English interpreter, the interpretation from B/C/S into English was corrected for us because there was a mistake. Since you, I take it, read the B/C/S and listen to the B/C/S, it has no impact on your understanding of the question. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, why did you call Mr. Vukovic a traitor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said it because he accused the Serb side of committing ethnic cleansing, whereas Mandic is indirectly denying it and saying that the man is a Serb. I'm saying he is a traitor if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter does not understand this. Could Mr. Krajisnik please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the interpreters had difficulties in translating what you said. Could you please resume where you said, "I am saying he is a traitor if --" and then continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this telephone conversation, Mr. Mandic tells me that Vukovic is a Serb and that he is accusing the Serb side, in other words him, of committing ethnic cleansing, and Mandic curses, mentioning his mother, and says that it's not true. And then I say, "What a traitor," because Mr. Mandic denied the accusation. And let me just add: At that time, there was a great desire on the part of civilians, women and children and others, to move from one part of town to the other, and I mean primarily Serbs, and that wish wasn't granted to them. They did not have the freedom of movement to move to safer territory. That is why I uttered that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And where is it in the conversation that Mr. Mandic says that it's not true?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you straight away. When he says -- I'm very sorry that I have to use this language. He said it here, fuck his mother and so on. He is cursing his mother because the man is accusing us, and he doesn't want to go on, go forward with the exchanges, because he views exchanges as ethnic cleansing. He doesn't want to go forward with the exchanges because he sees them as ethnic cleansing, and before that, Mandic says that they are not interested in prisoners anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, where now does Mr. Mandic - because that was the question - say that it's not true? If you curse someone's mother, it could mean a lot of things, isn't it? It could mean, well, I'm not very happy because he says what actually happens, or I'm not very happy because he is -- he is not telling the truth. It could be anything. So therefore, when Mr. Tieger asked you where does Mr. Mandic say that it's not true, I at least, in your answer, have not found the place, and the mere reference to the cursing of his mother could mean anything. So perhaps, if you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the way I understand it, and the way I understood it then, Your Honour, is this: They don't want exchanges, they only want ammunition and meat. And then he cursed the man's mother. That's how I understood it. He says that's ethnic cleansing. That's how I understood it then and how I understood it then [as interpreted]. He says they are interested only in ammunition and meat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least how Mr. Mandic translates -- let's not further comment on it. It's -- I've carefully listened to your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mandic interprets it that way. I was not abreast of what they were doing there. The point of this conversation were the two persons to be released. All the rest is just by the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But by the way is -- whether it's on the way or by the way, it's there. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you made reference quite a number of times, in fact, to events in August of 1992 in connection with the camps in -- the Serb-controlled camps in Bosnia. Can we agree or do you contest that the focus on camps in August, the attention paid to it by Bosnian Serb officials and by the Bosnian Serb leadership, occurred only after and in the wake of an international outcry about camps following the entry into Omarska by the international media and the worldwide dissemination of information about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. No. And I'll tell you why that is the case, and I said that a few moments ago as well. Ostojic took those journalists there. That is to say, that before that they had received information that everything was fine. So then they later established a commission to find out what was going on. I didn't know about it at the time but I see it now. It's all in documents now. They said that these newspapers were not telling the truth. I presented today the press release of the government. I'm saying what is contained in documents and what I heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, are you trying -- let me see if we have this straight. You're trying to tell the Court that this was a proactive, humanitarian effort by the Bosnian Serb leadership to -- to what, find out what was happening in the camps, establish what was happening in the camps and so they decided to bring the media along?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The journalists wanted to visit the prisons and that was made possible to them in the presence of Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Bozanic, and they toured all the prisons and they met up with the military. The conclusion of Ostojic and Bozanic was positive. You have their statements. And the journalists afterwards wrote nothing but the worst, and after that came the press release of the government. That's what I know from that time. Then they established commissions to establish what the actual state of affairs was. I'll bring you Mr. Ostojic's statement tomorrow. I'll find it somewhere. The one about the journalists. From that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is correct that, by the end of June -- end of July 1992, there was increasing pressure on the Bosnian Serb leadership about the mounting suspicion by the international community that large numbers of Muslims and Croats were being held in Serb detention facilities. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that terrible accusations were made by the international community in contacts with our representatives. Well, not terrible accusations but accusations, yes. And that is why they were sent to visit all the camps or prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And before the entry into those camps, the officials running the camps were notified and told to prepare the camps in so far as possible because the journalists were on their way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about that, and I never did anything about that in my own line of work. I only heard about it later when they came back. They reported to us that everything was fine. Or, rather, not that everything was fine but that their opinion was that everything was fine. That was the first time Ostojic and Bozanic were in those prisons too. I did not receive information that everything had been prepared in advance. On the contrary, that they paid a visit with the journalists and everything was fine over there, what they saw there. My impression was that that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have the next item distributed, please? And this will need a number, Your Honour, when the Registry and Court gets it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1247, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1247 is an urgent and confidential communication by General Mladic to the commander personally, giving an order in light -- in the goal of preparation of the POW camps for visits and making possible for journalists and members of the International Red Cross to visit them. And the order indicates at item 1: Immediately undertake measures to arrange camps in your zones of responsibility and prepare them for visits by foreign journalists and International Red Cross team. 2, the plan is to visit the following camps: Omarska, Trnopolje in the zone of 1st Krajina Corps and Lukavica prison in the zone of Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Also prepare all other POW camps in your zone of responsibility. Item 3, General Mladic indicates that they will be informed of the precise time of the visits. And turning the page, item 5 provides that, prepare material evidence regarding the crimes done by the enemy and present it in appropriate manner to those teams. Video tapes, photographs, objects, and so on. Now, among other things, Mr. Krajisnik, this again indicates that Omarska was anything but a secret camp. Correct? At least not a secret to -- within Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order from Mr. Mladic. This is the first time I see this. I can't even read it. But I'm telling you. Well, I mean, I can make no comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you want to read it, of course -- oh, you mean it's illegible. Any better copy available for Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard it. I listened to it. You don't really have to make that much of an effort. I believe that this is correct. But this is the first time that I see this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik has said that, "I can make no comments," is what it says in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that that is indeed what Mr. Krajisnik said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed. I'm sorry, and I have just said that that is what Mr. Krajisnik had just said and that is his answer to the question. In my submission, frankly, Your Honour, is a question like that calls for an answer such as the one Mr. Krajisnik has just given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I, as a matter of fact, I was -- I was listening, not reading at that time, and I must have understood that, perhaps wrongly, that Mr. Krajisnik said, "I can't even read it." Yes. "I can't even read it." And then he says, "I can make no comments." Of course my concern was that not having been able to read it, that that would contribute to not being able to make comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm very grateful for that. Perhaps Your Honour could clarify with Mr. Krajisnik whether he meant no comment because he couldn't read it, or no comment because the question was not one that he could comment upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You followed what Mr. Josse just said, Mr. Krajisnik. You also said that you heard what Mr. Tieger was saying. It was -- it was -- which you said I'd like to read it in order to see whether I can make any comment, or would you like to leave it as it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not necessary for me to read it. I've already said I heard what Mr. Tieger said, and my answer is that I cannot comment upon this because this is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, can't say that this is now an uninformed decision. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm sure it's not intended by my learned friend, but I just want to caution against objections that have any tendency to suggest to the witness what his answer might be to further inquiries by either the Prosecution or the Court. And I will say that the implications of -- the reason these questions are being put, in part, is because of Mr. Krajisnik's position, and the suggestion that -- I mean, he's free to say he has no comment, but the questions are completely appropriate and any suggestion -- I reject any suggestion to the contrary, and I think it's -- they are misplaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't understand Mr. Josse's comments at this moment as any criticism to your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that true, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I could argue with what my learned friend has just said but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not your intention --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you alluded to the discrepancy between the view of the camp by Mr. Ostojic and another gentleman you mentioned, and the view of the camps by the members of the international media and other representatives of the international community who entered the camps. So I -- is it fair to say that's a reflection of what I had mentioned earlier, that is, the international outcry that followed the dissemination of information about Omarska on approximately August 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the 5th of August is after Mr. Ostojic's visit. Let me just clarify that and then you can put your question. So it came after Mr. Ostojic's visit, as far as I can remember. And then please go ahead with your question so I will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What camp or camps did Mr. Ostojic visit?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely in Prijedor. And in Kozarski Vjesnik he gave that interview. You have it. It's in your material. I would have to look it up. Kozarski Vjesnik, he gave an interview that was entitled without censorship. He had a press conference with members of the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then let's examine what occurred after the visit to Omarska by the international journalists and the dissemination, internationally, of that information. So can I ask you to turn to tab 301, first?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1248, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1248 is a press release dated the 7th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one that I submitted today. That's the document that I was talking about. This one. That they were denying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What do you mean "they were denying it"? You mean the Republika Srpska government -- Republika Srpksa authorities were denying it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government, the government. I meant the government. The government was denying it after the visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting that the government was speaking solely on behalf of itself or essentially presenting the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership generally regarding Omarska camp and the other camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not abreast of this when the government made this statement. The government did this on the basis of their minister's visit to Omarska and their report to the government. Their press release was autonomous. I saw it here. I hadn't seen it before. I heard about all of this from them. I was not there. I did not hear anything. I didn't hear from foreign journalists. I mean I heard about it from Ostojic, the government, what the position was. They were criticising CNN here, that was not doing its work objectively, as they had put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This occurred a day after a Presidency session at which Mr. Djeric and you were present and in which the issues concerning Omarska were -- and other camps were discussed. Was there anything about this press release with which you disagreed, which you thought should have been added or omitted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, well, I know what is contained in the press release but I don't know what this is concretely. I mean, if you were to give me this record, perhaps I could make a comment. They wrote this themselves, probably on the basis of their own insight. May I get that record and then I can comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the press release first, Mr. Krajisnik. Dr. Djeric begins by noting, in the first full paragraph, he's -- he cites the unforgettable image of what he describes as a thin man. And then says that it was not even noted that there were not any women and children among the imprisoned, that all prisoners were men fit for military service. What's the significance of that focus, Mr. Krajisnik, that they were men fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that CNN had said that there were women and children there and that this was his response. And then the thin man, well, I don't know. He thought that they were only prisoners. That was his position on the basis of seeing people who were there. I'm not ruling out the possibility that it was different, but I'm just telling you what kind of information was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we continue on to page 4 of the English, and page 8 -- 9886 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, the press release continues: "Competent organs will present to the public data and evidence that will prove that the persons imprisoned in Omarska have taken part in armed combats against the army of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Where did Dr. Djeric get that information and what did he tell you and the other persons gathered at the Presidency meeting the day before about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he said at that session. I cannot remember. I can just assume that he got this from those who were there, and those who were there got it from those who were from Prijedor. I assume. There is no other way. And down here, he says the conditions are not proper because the other side does not want to have an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's another reflection of the exchange problem that we discussed earlier, being cited again by Dr. Djeric. Now, what information did you have about the imprisonment of persons in Omarska over the age of 60, heavily wounded and sick?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Karadzic had issued instructions to release persons over the age of 60. Probably this information was that there were some elderly people there. I assume. I cannot remember exactly what the information was at the time. However, what was carried out was based on information -- or, rather, as far as the negative things are concerned, orders were issued to -- well, at least in my presence, there was not a situation when something impermissible was referred to and when it was not said subsequently that that should be corrected. I mean, I'm just speaking off the cuff now, but it has to be contained in these conclusions as well. There were some decisions that were passed by those under whose jurisdiction this was. Well, if you have the record, you will see that that is the way it was. Probably, I don't know. I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate time, but I see the Court is looking at the transcript and may not wish to adjourn immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. There is no specific reason. I was looking for another matter. We'll adjourn until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think Mr. Josse would like to raise a few matters, but the Chamber it would like to turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before I given you an opportunity to briefly address the Court in relation to the scheduling of re-examination, I'd first like to deliver a statement of the Chamber on the submission of photographic material. I'd like to address the parties regarding the photographic material on destruction of property. On the 12th of June, after having reviewed the material, the Defence stated in court that they were not in a position to confirm the information provided in the explanatory schedule accompanying the photographs. The Chamber requests the Prosecution to provide the source of the information contained in the four columns of the explanatory schedule entitled municipality, location, object, and date destroyed to the extent that the source can be specified in a non-argumentative manner. The Chamber notes the concern of the Defence regarding the column entitled evidence/information in which the Prosecution links each photograph with other evidence in this case. This information should not be left in and the Chamber will make its own links and draw its own conclusions regarding the material. If the Prosecution wishes to present these links in its final written briefs, they may do so. But the Chamber reminds the parties of the limited purpose of these visualisations. Then the Defence indicated Mr. Krajisnik would also like to address Chamber regarding this material. The Chamber invites Mr. Krajisnik to raise his objections by clearly specifying the particular photograph and his concern and to be ready to do so by the first court session on Wednesday, the 28th of June. With regard to the related CD containing material on destruction of property, the Defence inquired about the commentary which accompanies the video and asked whether the Chamber would view the CD without listening to the audio. The Prosecution had no objection to this. The Chamber will therefore refrain from listening to the audio. The Prosecution is invited to submit the material to the registrar who is directed to assign provisional exhibit numbers and to inform the parties and the Chamber accordingly. This concludes this statement. And just for you, Mr. Krajisnik, when -- you'll have an opportunity to raise objections against these photographic material, the Chamber expects you not to reopen the whole of the debate on whether more damage was done elsewhere or who is to be responsible for the damage. I mean, what we expect, as a matter of fact, is that, for example, you say, look at this photograph, I clearly recognise this to be Doboj, and you can see there is a road sign there saying Doboj, and it's presented as Sarajevo material. That is the kind of comment we would expect you to give and not to open a debate on material which mainly serves to visualise what is established or is perhaps established, at least material -- to materialise -- to visualise damage which is supported by other evidence. If that's clear to you, then, Mr. Josse, I'll give you an opportunity now to address the Chamber on the re-examination matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, as I mentioned earlier, the Defence had assumed that the questions from the Bench in relation to this particular witness would come before re-examination. This assumption, and I accept it is an assumption, was based on how we saw the timetable as having been constructed. In particular, we would invite the Chamber to examine what was said on the 23rd of May of this year, at the very top of page 24605 of the transcript: "From that day on, the cross-examination and the questions by the Judges will take together no more than 15 days." And similarly, on the 30th of May, at page 24899: "And we were talking in about in 15 days, what has not been done yet is 15 days was for Prosecution and Chamber. We have not made a division there yet."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine you don't have to -- I'm not blaming the Defence at all for being confused about it. And that is -- you understand, this is an understatement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour. Could I be very frank? We would much rather, of course, re-examine later rather than earlier. Having said that, being as helpful as I can, if the Chamber, in effect, insists that I, because it will be me, tomorrow, start this re-examination, then I will go through as much of the material that Mr. Krajisnik has presented as I think is prudent. The Chamber has said, and I don't, with respect, criticise the Chamber for this at all, that it's up to the parties to decide whether to deal with this material. Well, frankly, Your Honour, the Prosecution were never going to deal with it to any great extent. Understandably. It's material that the witness has produced. Their time is extremely limited, and by its nature it was material that would likely, at least I hope it's likely, to help the cause of the witness who is also the accused. So we will try and deal with it in as much detail as we can, but also, I hope, in a sensible way. So that is where I would start tomorrow, if I have to, but I do emphasise we would much rather go after the Bench, as far as this witness is concerned. We submit that he is an in a different category to any other witness in this case in this regard. That's putting it in a nutshell, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think I asked you to give an assessment of the time you thought you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say I would rather think it over for another night, we would accept that. But of course this Chamber has to schedule as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I suspect a day of -- a court day is what I have in mind. I also have a series of clearing up questions in my notebook, some of which I'll want to ask. Others of which I might be able to discard. And generally, Your Honour, Mr. Stewart and I need to decide on whether there are other wider issues we would like to return to that have been dealt with in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're assessment is one day, I don't think that it would find any objection by the Chamber. Of course, we have given it some thought as well, and we've also looked at the statistics in this respect, and so therefore, when further thinking about it and preparing for it, I would not encourage you to bring the time further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's also very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger. I think is there any -- other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, we will continue preparing this afternoon on the assumption that we do have to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And once, if we have -- if we have taken a decision, as always, the Chamber will try to communicate the decision even if not yet delivered in court, to you already so in order not to further -- to make it more difficult for you, being unaware or uncertain about certain matters but of course only once we have made up our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yet again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I know you indicated you wanted to look at the August 6th session of the Presidency. But before turning to that, I have to return to another tab that I went past earlier, and that's tab 283.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's P439, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, I mentioned that in connection with the June 26 intercept between you and Mr. Mandic during which Mr. Vukovic was discussed. And if I could first bring your attention to the upper left-hand corner of the first page. It has a fax printout on it, as you can see. The very top, Mr. Krajisnik, at the -- at the left, just to -- so you can see that that's a fax that was sent on the 26th of June, 1992. And as you can see, it's to the central commission for the exchange of persons. If you'll turn to the last page of the document, here you'll see it's stamped and signed "State Commission Chairman, Filip Vukovic," with an attachment which is not contained here, that is a list of prisoners from 1 through 3.441. And then in particular, Mr. Krajisnik, I wanted to bring your attention to page -- the bottom of page 4 of the English, it's the second-to-last paragraph of the fax, where Mr. Vukovic states: "We believe that, once your side has fulfilled the previously arranged exchanges, we should embark on the release of all imprisoned persons and detainees in accordance with the agreement reached at UNPROFOR on 9 June 1992. The attachment contains the list of" -- that's the attachment that we just referred to of the prisoners from 1 to 3.441. "The attachment contains the list of imprisoned persons and detainees according to our records. It is our opinion that once released, the detainees should be sent to their places of residence, i.e., to their domicile address. Otherwise, this would signify typical deportation, exile and ethnic cleansing of the area. Such persons should also be issued with appropriate certificates to prevent arrests for the second or third time." Mr. Krajisnik, I simply wanted to ask you this: Based on the date of the fax, the date of your conversation with Mr. Mandic and the substance of the allegation contained in the fax and related to you by Mr. Mandic, it would appear that this is the allegation to which Mr. Mandic was referring in his conversation with you. I simply wanted to know whether you agree, disagree or don't know.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. I didn't see this document before. And I don't know what kind of agreement they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn next, then, to tab 300, and my apologies to the interpreters by the way. I can see by the length of time we waited for the translation to Mr. Krajisnik, that I was speaking too fast. Tab 300 appears to need a number, Your Honour, but I don't believe that's likely to be the case. It's the 24th Session of the Presidency on 6 August, so I apparently do not have the exhibit number handy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 24th Presidency session should be P65, tab 187 and/or P583, tab 83.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I had indicated earlier that the day before the press release, which we looked at, that is the press release by Dr. Djeric regarding CNN broadcast of Omarska, that there had been a Presidency session. You indicated you wanted to look at that. This session was attended by Dr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, yourself, Dr. Koljevic and Mr. Djeric. The last -- I will call it item on the agenda because many of them appear under item 2 but the last portion of that session seems to be devoted to the issue of prisoners detained in prisons in Serbian territory and a discussion about that. There is a discussion about their division into categories, and then the conclusion, well, discussion about the division into categories, pointing out that there should be compliance with international conventions, completely humane treatment of prisoners of war is advised, et cetera, and that food, clothes, are made at our expense and then there is a conclusion, "The Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be ordered to examine through its municipal branches the behaviour of all civilian authorities and individuals guarding prisoners of war. The information will be passed to the MUP which will be -- which will pass it on to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, is that the order to investigate what the situation with prisoners and detainees in facilities run by the Serbian authorities, to which you've been referring, or to which you referred earlier at various times, that is the Presidency asked the MUP to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's related to that statement by the Prime Minister, that there are some inhumane -- I mean, that the accommodation of prisoners is not good, et cetera. We had just had that report, the press release or the communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've referred earlier I think to the very firm stand taken by the Presidency and strict action or resolute action in response to information about the camps. What was the -- what was the MUP directed to do? What was the focus and purpose of their investigation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just repeat, and that is that. There was a standing instruction to investigate all irregularities, to punish perpetrators or offenders and to improve the accommodation for prisoners. There was always a positive reaction to reports and measures were taken. That's what I have been saying. There was not a single meeting wherein measures failed to be taken and there was a failure to respond to reports of irregularities. At least none that I attended. I don't know who wrote those instructions, that order. Maybe the Prime Minister. I mean, this order from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So we can -- you mentioned that so that we can see the Presidency's attitude toward camps through the investigations that followed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that there was this visit made to those camps -- prisons, rather, and certain irregularities were found. That's what the Prime Minister referred to in his report, insufficient space, inadequate accommodation, conditions, et cetera. And that's probably what the reaction of the Presidency was, namely that it should be investigated. All I remember is that the Presidency reacted in no uncertain terms that they wanted it investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at tab 305, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's P529, tab 295, P583, tab 90.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a commission that went to visit, on instructions from the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a quick look at that report. First of all, the commission members of that report were Vojin Bera, as we see at the end, Vaso Skondric, Ranko Mijic, and Jugoslav Rodic. And we can turn back, if necessary, to -- my recollection, Mr. Krajisnik, is that Mr. Ranko Mijic was one of the persons responsible for the work and categorisation of detainees according to the Drljaca order of or report to the CSB Banja Luka of 31 May 1992. "A mixed group consisting of national, public, and military security investigators shall be responsible for the work with and categorisation of detainees, they shall organise themselves respecting the parity principle. Mirko Jesic, Ranko Mijic --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise. Can you give us the reference in B/C/S? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's tab 262, item number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I was lending in Lieutenant Colonel Majsterovic shall be responsible for their work. Mr. Krajisnik, does that strike you as something of a problem, that one of the four persons on the commission established to investigate irregularities in Omarska, among other places, was one of the persons involved in the operation of the facility and who might himself have been responsible for such irregularities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what Mijic's function was. I mean, I cannot remember -- well, possibly you're right. I cannot remember now who Mijic was and what position he held. If he was that, then it's not right for him to be on the commission to investigate, if he was one of the perpetrators. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's go to the substance of the report, if we can. On page 4, under the general title of "reception centres in the municipality," that's page 4 of the English, and also page -- begins at page 4 of your version, then it moves on to page 5. The commission describes what happened in Omarska in respect to the what he calls their investigations. "After completing their investigations," the report states, "the operatives engaged would, depending on the results, sort the persons who had been brought in into three categories, according to the degree of their personal responsibility in the armed rebellion. Category 1 consisted of persons suspected of the gravest crimes, that is people who had directly participated in or organised the -- what he calls the armed rebellion. Category 2, persons suspected of assisting in arming. And category 3, persons who were captured in and brought in from areas where there had been fighting but had happened to be there because their extremists had prevented them from withdrawing to a secure place. During the investigation, no material evidence was found that they had in any way taken part in the armed rebellion." So that's another reflection, Mr. Krajisnik, of the rounding up of Muslims and Croats and their placement into detention facilities, irrespective of whether or not they had participated in what is referred to here as an armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, there is nothing for me to interpret here. I mean, I don't know what the situation was, and I cannot interpret it in any other way but the way in which this is written. It says that these persons were found there, they couldn't get out and there was no evidence of them having taken part in the rebellion. Now, is it women, children, old people? Is it able-bodied men? I don't know. I mean, that's not written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, of course if you ask Mr. Krajisnik whether that's another reflection of it, I mean, if he says yes, then it confirms what is there in writing. If he says -- of course, he could explain that. But, Mr. Krajisnik, if you have no specific knowledge on the matter, you can just say, "I read what it is. I have no further comment on it."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I have no knowledge. I just read what is written here. And I explained what the possible variance could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps then an answer in terms of "I have no further knowledge or comment than by reading it," then that would sufficiently clarify the matter. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik I've looked through this report. I don't see any, and I'd ask to you point me to any, reflection of an effort to determine what happened to the detainees during the course of their detention, what crimes were committed against them, how long they languished in detention, notwithstanding the fact that they were -- that they had not participated in any way in what is called an armed rebellion. Can you point me to any part of the report that indicates in any way that either an investigation of a criminal responsibility for their detention or for their treatment while in detention was undertaken or that measures of punishment were recommended?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say what measures were taken and whether any measures were taken at all. I don't know about that. I know what happened at the Presidency, that all of this should be investigated. This is a partial report that was made by a central commission, and then they informed the Presidency later on. That's Avlijas and everybody else. I don't have any other knowledge. As to whether they punished people, how and in which way, I don't know about that. Sorry, this is just the first insight of an official commission in these areas, from the outside, that is. It's a different matter that the police in Prijedor probably knew about what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, was there anything in the report, that is this report, and we'll turn to the other two reports you mentioned in a moment, anything in this report with which you found fault or disagreed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these reports misled me because I thought that Trnopolje was an open collection centre where people were seeking shelter. That's what I said to the Presiding Judge. Everybody was saying, and you can see these reports, that this was an open centre. And later on, I realised that there were killed persons there, raped persons there and so on and so forth. So that's the information that I received. And also, they were transferred to the open centre of Trnopolje. That's what is written here. Those who were not supposed to be processed any further. That's the information that I received about Trnopolje at the time when this was being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to verify, were you also misled, in view of Omarska and Keraterm? I mean, it says in very neutral terms, for example, that food was prepared in the Omarska and so-and-so kitchen. I mean about conditions in Omarska, did you -- did you think that this was a misleading report as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I never saw this report. The Prosecutor asked me whether there was something here that I had a different view about. And I said that it was only Trnopolje. Because before that, I had information that it was an open centre; whereas later on, here, I found out that it was an unfree prison, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you must have had the impression from this report, by reading it, that Omarska was fine as well. They had enough showers, food was prepared, basic medical protection was provided; whereas you may have heard some evidence by now, and it's not an adjudicated fact, that this was misleading as well. So I'm just a bit surprised that you say it's misleading in respect of Trnopolje for this and this reason on the basis of what I now have heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we just clarify, Your Honour? Question relates to Mr. Krajisnik's state of knowledge now? Is that right? Not in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I do understand from Mr. Krajisnik's testimony that at the time he thought of Trnopolje as an open reception centre, and he says now, by reading, "I didn't see the report at that time," I think he said, but reading it now, it's -- I must say it's misleading because I -- the report says it's an open reception centre where I now hear evidence that it's not. And then it surprised me that Mr. Krajisnik only mentions Trnopolje in this respect since we've heard not only evidence but we have even an adjudicated facts which one would be inclined to qualify as such that would make this report misleading in respect of those facilities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand. I think Mr. Krajisnik does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please, I mean, really, I hadn't read the entire report, and I saw Trnopolje and that's why I reacted. I mean, if you were to ask me now, of course, that was wrong, it was misguiding. Had I read it then, I would have said Omarska was all right. But I hadn't read this so that's why I didn't react. I mean, I didn't read it here and now. I mean, I simply happened to glance at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said, "I hadn't read the entire report and I saw Trnopolje." Are you talking about -- just looking at it because it is in evidence of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am clear that Mr. Krajisnik means literally now. Now in the last few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's clear. You say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... casting an eye on it at this moment and seeing Trnopolje described as an open reception centre, that that certainly was misleading and, yes, I now do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the only thing I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's time for a break but if I could just ask one question before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, to your knowledge, who did receive and read this report by the commission related to Omarska and Trnopolje, Keraterm, camps in Sanski Most and other places in Western Bosnia and the Avlijas reports? Who received and made those reports to which you've been referring?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these reports here. I don't know whether I read it, but I first saw the last page. I don't know whether I managed to read the whole thing. I saw certain irregularities and perhaps I forgot a bit. As for Avlijas and his report, I don't remember that report either. But I saw it here and I read it here. There is a report from Eastern Herzegovina too. As for who else received it, I don't know. I mean, I saw it was there at the government session, among the papers, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Krajisnik, I'm instructing you not to speak with anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given, and we'll adjourn for the day and resume tomorrow morning, 9.00, in this same courtroom. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
